0: You download the model, then running it reports not enough memory or VRAM. That is probably the result most people least want to see when trying a local model.
1: As mentioned earlier, running a model needs its weights loaded into memory or VRAM, and generating answers takes extra space. If your device cannot fit the model, besides switching to a model with fewer parameters you can also look for a quantized version.
3: Model weights consist of a great many numbers, and storing each one takes space. Quantization reduces the model's resource footprint by lowering the precision used to represent those numbers. For example, weights originally stored as 16-bit floats are converted to a mostly 8-bit or 4-bit low-precision representation. The number of parameters usually stays the same; the space each parameter takes gets smaller.

14: For an ordinary user, the most direct benefit of quantization is a smaller model file: downloads and storage take less space, and the weights occupy less memory or VRAM at run time. Where the hardware and inference framework support it well, quantization may also improve inference speed.
15: Still, shrinking the file to a quarter of its size does not mean the answers get four times faster.
16: Lower precision can also affect answer quality, and how much depends on the model, the quantization method and the task. When choosing a quantized version, besides confirming it runs, try it on the questions you care about and see whether the answers are still reliable.
18: For a model you have already downloaded or fine-tuned, the common approach is post-training quantization (PTQ): after training is finished, convert the weights and other numbers to a lower-precision representation. Some methods need a small batch of representative data to calibrate the quantization process and keep the error as small as possible.
19: The other family is quantization-aware training (QAT), which simulates the effect of quantization during training so the model gets used to low-precision representation in advance.
20: This chapter covers the GGUF quantized models common in local running, to help you read the files, tell the versions apart and make a choice. The concrete steps for other quantization methods will be added later.
22: When running models with Ollama you often see names such as GGUF, Q4 and Q8. These relate mainly to the model's storage format and quantization method, and they are an important reason large models can run on a personal computer.
23: In August 2023 Georgi Gerganov introduced the GGUF format, whose main advantages include single-file deployment, extensibility, memory-mapped support, complete information and ease of use. A GGUF file contains a header, metadata key-value pairs and tensor information, among other things. Together these define the model's structure and behaviour, as shown below: GGUF is a model file format for large-model inference, now widely used by local inference tools such as llama.cpp and Ollama. Ollama wraps up the GGUF format, model quantization and model loading, so users need not convert the format themselves and can download and run already-quantized models directly. A GGUF file holds not only the model parameters but also basic model information, the model structure and tensors. GGUF organises this information in a single unified file format so inference tools such as llama.cpp can read and load it directly, as the figure below shows.

25: GGUF itself is only a model file format and does not by itself reduce a model's memory and VRAM footprint. What actually reduces resource use is quantization.
27: In llama.cpp and GGUF models, Q4, Q5, Q8 and Q4_K_M are different quantization names. Q stands for quantization and the number after it is the main quantization bit width: Q4 means mostly 4-bit quantization, Q8 mostly 8-bit.
28: Note that Q4 does not mean every parameter in the model uses a uniform 4-bit representation. Take the common Q4_K_M: it is one of llama.cpp's K-quant types. In the name, Q4 means mostly 4-bit quantization, K means the K-quant scheme and M means the Medium configuration within that scheme. In a real model, different tensors may use different quantization precisions rather than every parameter using a uniform 4-bit representation, as shown below.
30: When choosing a GGUF model, first confirm the inference tool supports it, then look at the specific quantized version. Lower precision usually reduces memory and VRAM use, making the model easier to run on ordinary hardware, but may lose some quality; higher precision usually preserves more of the original model's ability while needing more hardware resources.
31: If a version is already close to your device's memory or VRAM limit, consider one with a smaller footprint to leave headroom for the context and the run itself. If resources allow, compare answers from different versions on the same questions, paying particular attention to the task you need, such as information extraction, code generation or strictly formatted output.
32: Confirm it runs reliably first, then check answer quality. A quantized version chosen that way suits your device and purpose better.
